body_md:
\label{remark 2.3}
The corresponding Riemann invariant obtained from $\bar z(y)$, namely $\bar z(t,x) = \delta (-t)^{\delta-1} \bar z (y)  $ (cf. \eqref{selfsimilar ansatz})                                 
 at given initial time $t_0<0$       
 near the vacuum boundary   
takes the from 
$$ \bar z(t_0,x) =  \tfrac{4}{(\gamma+1)t_0} x + c_1 x^{\beta}+ o(x^{\beta}), \quad 0<x\ll 1 $$ 
where $c_1>0$ is an arbitrary constant;                                     
as $t\to 0^-$ and $x>0$, it takes the form $$ \bar z(t,x) = - c_2 x^{1-\mu} + o(|t|), \quad x>0, \ |t|\ll 1 $$
 for some $c_2>0$.

label: prop bar z
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $(1)$, since $\bar z = -2y\bar U$, we compute
\[
    \partial_y \bar z = -2\Bigl(\bar U + y\,\partial_y \bar U \Bigr)
    = -2\Biggl(\bar U - \frac{[(\gamma+1)\bar U - 2\mu]\bar U}{(\gamma+1)\bar U-2}\Biggr)
    = \frac{-4(\mu-1)\bar U}{(\gamma+1)\bar U - 2}.
\]
Since the function $g(r) = \frac{-4(\mu-1)r}{(\gamma+1)r - 2}$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $r\in[0, \frac{2\mu}{\gamma+1}]$ and $\bar U(y)$ is strictly decreasing from $\frac{2\mu}{\gamma+1}$ to $0$ as $y$ increases from $0$ to $\infty$, $ \partial_y \bar z$ is increasing from $\partial_y \bar z(0)=-\frac{4\mu}{\gamma+1}$ to $\lim_{y\to \infty} \partial_y \bar z(y)=0$.

For $(2)$, one finds
\[
    1+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\,\partial_y \bar z
    = \frac{(2-\mu)\bar U - \tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}{\bar U - \tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}.
\]
The function $f(r)=\frac{(2-\mu)r-\tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}{r-\tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}$ is decreasing for $r\in\bigl[0,\tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}\mu\bigr]$. Since $\bar U$ is decreasing in $y$, it follows that
\[
    1-\mu = \frac{(2-\mu)\bar U(0) - \tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}{\bar U(0)-\tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}
    < 1+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\,\partial_y \bar z
    \leq \lim_{y\to\infty} \frac{(2-\mu)\bar U(y) - \tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}}{\bar U(y)-\tfrac{2}{\gamma+1}} = 1,
\]
where we used \eqref{Asy at C} in the last equality.

For $(3)$, the expansion \eqref{z y<<1} follows directly from \eqref{Asy at C}. Since $\beta \geq 2$, the bounds on $\partial_y \bar z$ and $\partial_y^2 \bar z$ are immediate. For higher-order derivatives, note that $\bar z \in C^{\infty}$ if $\mu \in \mathfrak S$, and $\bar z \in C^{[\beta],\beta-[\beta]}$ if $\mu \notin \mathfrak S$. This explains the dichotomy in \eqref{payi z y<<1}. A direct computation yields the stated bounds.

For $(4)$, the asymptotics \eqref{z y>>1} follow from \eqref{Asy at A}, and the derivative estimates \eqref{payi z y>>1} are then straightforward.

name: Weighted $L^2$ estimates

title: Proof
body_md:
We start with the estimation of $\frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{Z }{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2$. Using the $Z$ equation in \eqref{linear PDE of tilde z w} and integrating by parts, we first obtain 
	\begin{align*}
		\frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{Z }{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 &= \int_0^\infty -(y+\frac{\gamma+1}{4} \mathring z) y^{-2{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}Z \partial_y Z -  (\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\partial_y \mathring z +\mu-1)|\frac{Z}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}|^2 \ dy \\
        &\quad - \int_0^\infty   \frac{3-\gamma}{4}\partial_y \mathring z {y^{-2{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}{W Z}  \ dy
		+\int_0^\infty  
        y^{-2{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}F_1 {Z}{}  \ dy 
		 \\ &\leq   \int_0^\infty   \Big(-(1+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\frac{\mathring z}{y}){\bf{n}_{\mu}}+\frac32-\mu-\frac{\gamma+1}{8} \partial_y\chi \bar z-\frac{\gamma+1}{8} \chi\partial_y \bar z \Big) |\frac{Z}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}|^2 \ dy \\
		 &\quad + \frac12 \left| \langle  \partial_y \mathring z \frac{W}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}, \frac{Z}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \rangle \right| + \left| \langle \frac{F_1}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},\frac{Z}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \rangle\right|   
         \end{align*}
      Since $\partial_y\chi \bar z\ge 0$ and $1+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\frac{\mathring z}{y} \ge 1- \mu $, $|\partial_y \bar z |\le \frac{4\mu}{\gamma +1} $ by Proposition \ref{prop bar z}, and by using the Young's inequality for the second crossing term, we deduce that for any small $\varepsilon>0$,   
         \begin{align*}
         \frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{Z }{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2  
		& \leq  \Big(-(1-\mu){\bf{n}_{\mu}}+\frac32-\frac{1}{2}\mu+\epsilon\Big) \left\lVert\frac{Z}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 +C_\varepsilon \left\lVert\frac{W}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 + \left| \langle \frac{F_1}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},\frac{Z}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \rangle\right| .  
	\end{align*} 
Similarly, we compute $\frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{W}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 $
	\begin{align*}
		\frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{W}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 &= \int_0^\infty -(y+\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\mathring z )y^{-2{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}W \partial_y W - (\mu-1)|\frac{W}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}|^2\ dy+ \int_0^\infty   
        y^{-2{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}F_2 {W}  \ dy \\
		&\leq \int_0^\infty\Big( -(1+\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\frac{\mathring z}{y} ){\bf{n}_{\mu}} +\frac{3}{2}-\mu+\frac{3-\gamma}{8}\partial_y \mathring z \Big) |\frac{W}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}|^2\ dy+\left| \langle \frac{F_2}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},\frac{W}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \rangle\right|.
	\end{align*}
    Observe that $1+\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\frac{\mathring z}{y} \ge 1 - \frac{3-\gamma}{1+\gamma}\mu$,  $\partial_y \mathring z\le \partial_y \chi \bar z$, and also  $|\partial_y \chi \bar z|\le c/y_{0}^\mu $ for some $c>0$ that follows from 
    Proposition \ref{prop bar z} and Lemma \ref{le: supp chi}. Hence by taking $y_0$ large enough that $ \frac{3-\gamma}{8} c/y_{0}^\mu \le \mu /2$,  we deduce that
    \begin{align*}
		\frac12 \partial_\tau\left\lVert\frac{W}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 
		&\leq\Big( -(1-\frac{3-\gamma}{\gamma+1}\mu ){\bf{n}_{\mu}} +\frac{3}{2}-\frac\mu2 
        \Big)  \left\lVert\frac{W}{y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}}\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 +\left| \langle \frac{F_2}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},\frac{W}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \rangle\right|
	\end{align*}
     Recall the definition of ${\bf{n}_{\mu}}$ in \eqref{def ndmu}. Choose small enough $\varepsilon_0>0$ and then sufficiently large $b>0$ such that 
    \[
    -(1-\frac{3-\gamma}{\gamma+1}\mu ){\bf{n}_{\mu}} +\frac{3}{2}-\frac{\mu}{2} + \frac{C_{\epsilon_0}}{b}  < -(1-\mu){\bf{n}_{\mu}}+\frac32-\frac{1}{2}\mu+\epsilon_0 <0. 
    \]
    Combining the above two inequalities, we obtain the desired estimates.

label: reorde nmz
title: Proof
body_md:
From the definition of $M_z$ and $M_w$,  we claim that
    \[
        \partial_y^i\mathcal T_z(\tau,0) = \partial_y^i\mathcal T_w (\tau,0)=0
    \]
    for any $i\in\{0,1,{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1\}$. 
    To justify this, we expand $\mathcal T_z$ and $\mathcal T_w$ in powers of $y$, apply $\partial_y^i$ to the resulting expressions, and then evaluate at $y=0$. The terms that remain coincide exactly with the modulation equations for $(z_i,w_i)$ given in \eqref{ode of ziwi with z1=0}.
To illustrate the argument, we present the proof for $\mathcal T_z$, and the case of $\mathcal T_w$ follows analogously. 
    By recalling \eqref{nz nmz}, we rearrange $\mathcal T_z$ in terms of $y^i$: 
    \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\label{reorde nmz}
       \mathcal T_z &= \varphi\sum_{i=2}^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1}\frac{1}{i!}\Big(\partial_\tau z_i  + z_i (i +\mu-1)   +\sum_{\ell=2}^{i-1} \frac{\ell i!}{\ell! (i+1-\ell)!} z_{\ell}(\frac{3-\gamma}{4} w_{i+1-\ell}+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}z_{i+1-\ell}) \Big) y^i \\
        &+\varphi\sum_{i=2}^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1} \Big(\frac{z_i}{i!}(i\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\frac{\mathring z}{y}+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\partial_y \mathring z ) y^i +\frac{w_i}{i!}\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\partial_y \mathring z y^i\Big)  \\
        &+\partial_y\varphi\sum_{i=2}^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1}\frac{z_i}{i!} \Big((y+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}\mathring z) y^i+  (\frac{\gamma+1}{4}M_z+\frac{3-\gamma}{4}M_w) y^i
        \Big) \\
      &+ \varphi \sum_{i={\bf{n}_{\mu}}}^{2{\bf{n}_{\mu}} -3} \sum_{\ell=2}^{i-1} \frac{\ell i!}{\ell! (i+1-\ell)!} z_{\ell}(\frac{3-\gamma}{4} w_{i+1-\ell}+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}z_{i+1-\ell}) \Big) y^i
 \end{aligned}\end{equation}
    Let $m\in\{0,1,\dots,{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1\}$. We then apply $\partial_y^m$ to the above equation and evaluate at $y=0$:
    \begin{align*}
        \partial_y^m \mathcal T_z(\tau,0) &= \partial_\tau z_m + (i-1 -i\mu)z_m -\frac{(3-\gamma)\mu}{\gamma+1} w_m+  \sum_{\ell=2}^{m-2} \frac{\ell m!}{\ell! (m+1-\ell)!}z_\ell(\frac{3-\gamma}{4} w_{i-\ell}+\frac{\gamma+1}{4}z_{i-\ell}) \\
       &+\sum_{i=2}^{m-1}\frac{3-\gamma}{4}  \binom{m}{i} \partial_y^{m+1-i} \mathring z(0)w_i+  \binom{m}{i} \frac{\gamma+1}{4} \big(\partial_y^{m-i} \mathring z (0)z_{i+1}+ \partial_y^{m+1-i} \mathring z(0) z_i\big) =0 
    \end{align*}
       by using \eqref{ode of ziwi with z1=0}. By using the compactness of $\varphi$ and Proposition \ref{trapping} , the inequality holds for $i\in\{0,1,\dots,{\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1\}$. 
   We then proceed to derive the $L^2$ integrability of $\frac{\mathcal T_z}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}$ and $\partial_y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}} \mathcal T_z$. For $\mu\in \mathfrak S$, the statement holds trivially, since $\mathcal T_z$ is smooth and compactly supported. It therefore suffices to consider the case $\mu\notin \mathfrak S$. In \eqref{reorde nmz}, the first and fourth lines consist of monomials $y^i$ with integer $i$, while the third line vanishes at $y=0$ due to the factor $\partial_y\varphi$. Hence, these contributions are integrable. 
 The remaining terms in the second line involve $\partial_y \mathring z\, y^{i}$ and $\mathring z\, y^{i-1}$, which are only H\"{o}lder continuous for $y\ll 1$, since $\mathring z(y)\sim y+y^\beta$ as $y\ll 1$ by Proposition \ref{prop bar z}. These terms require separate treatment. 
 For $y\ll 1$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{\mathring z y^{i-1}}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},  \frac{\partial_y\mathring z y^{i}}{y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}},   \partial_y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \big(\mathring z y^{i-1} \big),\  \partial_y^{{\bf{n}_{\mu}}} \big(\partial_y \mathring z y^{i}\big) \sim y^{\beta+i-1-{\bf{n}_{\mu}}}.
   \end{align*}
 Since the initial modulation variables satisfy \eqref{initialziwi} and from ${\bf{n}_{\mu}}$ defined in \eqref{def ndmu}, we have $\beta+i-1-{\bf{n}_{\mu}} >-\frac12$ for $i\geq 2$, which ensures the square integrability.  This completes the proof.

The existence of a well-posed solution in $H^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}$ follows directly from Proposition \ref{bootstrap lemma} via a continuity argument. The decay estimate \eqref{decay fact} is a consequence of Proposition \ref{bootstrap lemma}, Proposition \ref{prop payi mz mw}, and Lemma             
\ref{Linfty decay}. Indeed, by using Lemma              
\ref{Linfty decay}, we have
\begin{align*}
    &\left\lVert\big(\partial_y\tilde z(\tau,\cdot)-\partial_y \mathring z(\tau,\cdot), \partial_y\tilde w(\tau,\cdot)\big)\right\rVert_{L^\infty} \\&\leq \left\lVert(\partial_yM_z,\partial_yM_w)\right\rVert_{L^\infty} + \left\lVert(\partial_yZ,\partial_yW)\right\rVert_{L^\infty} \\
    &\leq \left\lVert(\partial_yM_z,\partial_yM_w)\right\rVert_{L^\infty} + \left\lVert\big(\partial_yZ(\tau,\cdot), \partial_yW(\tau,\cdot)\big)\right\rVert_{L^2}^{1-\frac{1}{2({\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1)}}\left\lVert\big(\partial_y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}Z(\tau,\cdot), \partial_y^{\bf{n}_{\mu}}W(\tau,\cdot)\big)\right\rVert_{L^2}^{\frac{1}{2({\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1)}}\\
    & \lesssim e^{-\mathtt{a_0}\tau} + e^{-(\mu-\frac12)(1-\frac{1}{2({\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1)})\mathtt{a_2}\tau}e^{-\frac{\mathtt{a_1}}{2({\bf{n}_{\mu}}-1)}\tau}.
\end{align*}
where we have applied Proposition \ref{bootstrap lemma} and Proposition \ref{prop payi mz mw} to obtain the last inequality.
The statement on the finite codimensional stability follows directly from \eqref{boundary condition} of $I^{\lfloor \beta \rfloor}$ together with Proposition \ref{trapping}.

name: Proof of Theorem \ref{thm 4.1}

title: Proof
body_md:
Direct computation shows
    \begin{align*}
        \left\lVertz\right\rVert_{L^2_x}^2 &= \int_0^\infty z^2(t,x) \ dx = \int_0^\infty (\frac{1}{\mu})^{2\delta} e^{(2\mu-2)\tau}\hat z^2(\tau,y)(\frac{1}{\mu})^{\delta} e^{- \tau} \ dy = (\frac{1}{\mu})^{3\delta} e^{(2\mu- 3)\tau}\int_0^\infty \hat z^2(\tau,y) \ dy\\
       & \leq Ce^{(2\mu- 3)\tau} \big(\left\lVert\mathring z\right\rVert_{L^2}^2+\left\lVertM_z\right\rVert_{L^2}^2+\left\lVertZ\right\rVert_{L^2}^2 \big).
    \end{align*}
 By Proposition \ref{prop: mathring z}, Proposition \ref{prop payi mz mw}, together with the estimate \eqref{L2}, we obtain the $L^2$-boundedness of $z$. The same argument yields the boundedness of $\left\lVertw\right\rVert_{L^2_x}$. 
 Hence, we deduce the $L^2$ boundedness of $u$ and $c$. 
 
 The asymptotic behavior \eqref{1.7} is a direct consequence of \eqref{decay fact} and Proposition \ref{prop: mathring z}.
 
    The positivity of $\rho$ can be shown provided that the initial data has strictly positive density in the interior of the domain. Introducing the Lagrangian flow map defined by
    \[\frac{d}{dt}X(t,x) = u(t,X(t,x)),\quad X(t_0,x)=x,\]and integrating the first equation of \eqref{Euler} along the flow map, we have 
    \begin{align*}
                                                                                
        \rho(t,X(t,x)) = \rho(t_0,X(t_0,x)) e^{-\int_{t_0}^t u_x(s,X(s,x))ds}.
    \end{align*}
    Since the solution is smooth for $t_0<t<0$ 
    and the gradient blow-up occurs only at $(t,x)=(0,0)$, the density remains strictly positive in the interior of the domain.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first define $f_\lambda(y) = f(\lambda y)$ and compute 
	\[
		\int_{a}^{b} (\partial_y^i f(y))^2 \ dy = \lambda^{1-2i}\int_{ a/\lambda}^{b/\lambda} (\partial_y^i f_\lambda(y))^2 \ dy, \ \ \int_{a}^{b} y^{-2n} (f(y))^2 \ dy = \lambda^{1-2n}\int_{ a/\lambda}^{b/\lambda} y^{-2n} (f_\lambda(y))^2 \ dy.
	\] 
	 We then set $\lambda_j =  2^j y_*$, and define $f_j:=f_{\lambda_j}$ for $y\in[2^jy_*, 2^{j+1}y_*]$. Then, 
	 \begin{align*}
	 	\int_{y_*}^\infty y^{-2(n-i)} (\partial_y^i f)^2 \ dy 
        &\leq \sum_{j=0}^\infty \lambda_j^{1-2n}  \int_{1 }^{2}    (\partial_y^i f_j)^2 \ dy \\
		&\leq  \sum_{j=0}^\infty  \lambda_j^{1-2n}C_1 \Big( \left\lVert\partial_y^n f_j\right\rVert_{L^2([1,2])}^{\frac{2i}{n}}\left\lVertf_j\right\rVert_{L^2([1,2])}^{2-\frac{2i}{n}}+\left\lVertf_j\right\rVert_{L^2([1,2])} \Big)\\
        &\leq \sum_{j=0}^\infty C_1  \Big(  \left\lVert\partial_y^n f\right\rVert_{L^2([\lambda_j,2\lambda_j])}^{\frac{2i}{n}}\left\lVert y^{-n}f\right\rVert_{L^2([\lambda_j,2\lambda_j])}^{2-\frac{2i}{n}}+ \left\lVert y^{-n}f\right\rVert_{L^2([\lambda_j,2\lambda_j])}\Big) 
	 \end{align*}
     where we have used the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality in the second inequality.
     We then use the H\"{o}lder inequality on the first summation and together with Lemma \ref{hardy 1}, we deduce the result.

label: Linfty decay
title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Direct computation shows
    \begin{align*}
        (\partial_y^j f)^2 = \int_0^y 2\partial_y^j f \partial_y^{j+1} f d\tilde y.
    \end{align*}
    Hence, by using Holder inequality, we obtain
    \[
        \left\lVert\partial_y^j f\right\rVert_{L^\infty} \lesssim \left\lVert\partial_y^j f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left\lVert\partial_y^{j+1}f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{\frac{1}{2}}.
    \]
    By the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality
    \[
        \left\lVert\partial_y^jf\right\rVert_{L^2} \lesssim \left\lVert\partial_y f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{1-\frac{j-1}{n-1}} \left\lVert\partial_y^n f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{\frac{j-1}{n-1}}, \ \ \ 
        \left\lVert\partial_y^{j+1}f\right\rVert_{L^2} \lesssim \left\lVert\partial_y f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{1-\frac{j}{n-1}} \left\lVert\partial_y^n f\right\rVert_{L^2}^{\frac{j}{n-1}}, 
    \]
    we obtain the desired inequality.

$C^{[\frac{1}{1-\mu}], \frac{1}{1-\mu} - [\frac{1}{1-\mu}]}             
    $ only if $\mu\in\mathfrak S$ (cf. \eqref{eigenfunction}).                                   
     Moreover, when $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$, direct computation shows $\Lambda_v\bar z = -\frac{\gamma+1}{4} \Lambda_T \bar z$.
     Therefore, when $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$, the eigenfunctions associated with time translation and Galilean Transformation coincide.

title: Remark
body_md: Requiring one more degree of regularity at the critical values ($\mu \in \mathcal H$) induces non-integrable singular behavior  (in the sense of $L^2$) of interaction terms between low modulation variables and the profile itself. This motivates us to introduce one more constraint $w_2=0$, which  removes such logarithmical non-integrable singular behavior.

label: lemma w_1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will prove it by a continuity argument. Since the $w_1(0)=\epsilon_0$ is sufficiently small, $\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1(0)>0$ initially. Consequently, $\partial_\tau w_1(\tau_0)<0$. By the Picard–Lindelöf theorem, there exists $\nu_0 > 0$ such that the solution to the ODE \eqref{ode w_1} with initial condition $w_1(\tau_0) = \epsilon_0$ exists on the interval $\tau \in [\tau_0,\tau_0+\nu_0)$. Moreover, $\nu_0$ can be chosen sufficiently small so that $w_1(\tau_0)-w_1(\tau)\ll 1$. It then follows that 
	\[
		1-\frac{3-\gamma}{\gamma+1}\frac{\mu}{\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1}>0, \ w_1\in(0,\epsilon) \text{ for }\tau\in[\tau_0,\tau_0+\nu_0).
	\]
	In particular 
	\[
		\partial_\tau w_1<0\text{ for }\tau\in[\tau_0,\tau_0+\nu_0).
	\]
	By a standard continuity argument, the solution can be extended to all $\tau \in [\tau_0,\infty)$, and $w_1$ is strictly decreasing. Furthermore, note that $w_1 \equiv 0$ is itself a solution to the ODE \eqref{ode w_1}. By uniqueness of solutions guaranteed by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem, this establishes the second part of the statement. Now, we remain to show \eqref{estimate of w_1}. Since $w_1\in[0,\epsilon_0)$. Then, there exists an nonzero real number $\alpha$ such that
	\[
		\partial_\tau w_1 < -\alpha^2 w_1.
	\]
	It then follows                                    
    
                                                                                       
    
                                                                                                         
	\[
		w_1(\tau)< w_1(\tau_0)e^{-\alpha^2 (\tau-\tau_0)}.
	\]
	This completes the proof.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By using \eqref{ode of T'}, we compute
	\[
		T_\tau = e^{-\mu\tau} \frac{\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1}{\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1}<e^{-\mu\tau} \frac{\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0}{\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0},
	\]
	where we have used that $f(x) = \frac{x}{\mu-x}$ is an increasing function for $x\in[0,\mu)$ and $w_1$ is strictly decreasing from $\epsilon_0$ to 0 as proved in Lemma \ref{lemma w_1}. Hence, 
	\begin{equation}
		T_*  = \int_{\tau_0}^\infty e^{-\mu\tau} \frac{\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1(\tau)}{\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}w_1(\tau)} \ d\tau < \int_{\tau_0}^\infty e^{-\mu\tau} \frac{\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0}{\mu-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0} \ d\tau = \frac{\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0}{\mu^2-\frac{3-\gamma}{4}\epsilon_0\mu}< 2\epsilon_0,
	\end{equation}
	where we have used $\gamma\in(1,3)$ and $\mu\in[\frac12,1)$ in the last inequality.
